channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You take the credit and blame the world.
item.description: A 1975 study by Miller and Ross examined the self-serving bias, questioning whether the attribution of success to internal factors and failure to external ones is a defense mechanism or a byproduct of information processing.

item.title: You will change your answer to fit the group.
item.description: A 1951 study found that 74% of participants gave at least one incorrect answer to a simple task to match the majority.

item.title: You adopt the mood of the room without choosing.
item.description: A 1994 research review found that people automatically mimic the facial expressions and postures of those around them.

item.title: One positive trait blinds you to every other defect.
item.description: A 1920 study found that officers who rated a soldier highly in one category consistently rated them highly in all unrelated categories.

item.title: You exert less effort when you are not alone.
item.description: A 1913 study found that individuals pulling on a rope in a group exert less force than when pulling individually.

item.title: The more you try not to think, the more.
item.description: A 1994 study revealed that instructions to suppress a specific thought result in that thought becoming more cognitively accessible.

item.title: You judge others by their character, not their context.
item.description: A 1967 study found that people attributed views expressed in an essay to the writer's internal beliefs, even when told the writer had no choice in the topic.

item.title: A repeated claim eventually feels like a known truth.
item.description: A 2015 study found that even clearly false headlines are rated as more accurate simply because they have been seen before.

item.title: You believe the world is fundamentally fair to everyone.
item.description: A 1966 study demonstrated that people will blame victims for their own misfortune to maintain the belief that people generally get what they deserve.

item.title: You mistake your own point of view for objective reality.
item.description: Research indicates that people assume their view of the world is based on unbiased information, while those who disagree with them are biased by their ideology.

item.title: You continue losing ventures because of the investment already made.
item.description: A 1985 study found that people are more likely to continue investing in a failing project if they have already committed significant time or money to it.

item.title: A small favor makes a large request more likely.
item.description: A 1966 study found that people who agreed to a trivial request were significantly more likely to agree to a larger, related request a few days later.

item.title: You create obstacles to explain your potential failure.
item.description: A 1978 experiment showed that people who are uncertain about their performance will intentionally choose to hinder their own ability to succeed, such as by choosing a performance-impairing drug.

item.title: You value money differently depending on where it came from.
item.description: A 1985 study found that people treat funds differently—and are more likely to spend 'windfall' gains—even when the amount is logically identical to their earned income.

item.title: An audience changes your performance depending on the task difficulty.
item.description: A 1965 study demonstrated that the mere presence of others improves performance on simple tasks while hindering it on complex or unfamiliar ones.

item.title: You feel more in control when you participate in luck.
item.description: In a 1975 study, participants perceived a game based entirely on chance as a skill-based challenge simply because they were allowed to choose their own lottery ticket.

item.title: You believe generic personality descriptions are uniquely about you.
item.description: A 1948 study found that when individuals are given a vague, personality assessment, they overwhelmingly rate it as accurate to them personally.

item.title: You assess risks as lower because you feel good.
item.description: A 2000 study demonstrated that affective evaluation of an activity, influenced by information framing, causes inverse shifts in perceived risk and benefit.

item.title: You seek useless information just to feel more certain.
item.description: A body of research in judgment and decision-making, discussed in Jonathan Baron's 1988 book Thinking and Deciding, indicates that individuals often seek out information that has no impact on their decision to reduce uncertainty.

item.title: You cannot imagine what it is like not knowing.
item.description: A 1990 study by Elizabeth Newton found that individuals possess a 'curse of knowledge' that makes them systematically overestimate how easily others can perceive information they already know.

item.title: You only vividly remember the beginning and the end.
item.description: A 1962 experiment confirmed that memory recall is highest for items at the start and end of a list, with a significantly lower probability of recall for middle items.

item.title: A third option changes which of two items you prefer.
item.description: A 1982 study demonstrated that adding a clearly inferior third option makes a more expensive or premium item appear more attractive.

item.title: Asking if you will do a task makes it likelier.
item.description: A 1993 study showed that simply surveying people about their intention to perform a future behavior increases the likelihood they will do it.

item.title: You assume your future self wants what you want now.
item.description: A 2003 theoretical paper by Loewenstein, O'Donoghue, and Rabin formalized the concept of 'projection bias,' building on empirical findings like the 1998 study by Read and van Leeuwen.

item.title: You are convinced the outcome was predictable all along.
item.description: A 1975 study found that people consistently overestimate their ability to have foreseen an event once they know how it concluded.

item.title: You would not notice if your life changed suddenly.
item.description: A 2005 experiment demonstrated that people fail to identify when their expressed preferences are switched by an experimenter.

item.title: You only remember the one thing that stood out.
item.description: The Von Restorff effect is a demonstrated phenomenon where an isolated item in a list is more likely to be recalled than the other items.

item.title: You often misinterpret your own physical anxiety as attraction.
item.description: Heightened physical arousal from an external source is frequently mislabeled as intense romantic or social interest.

item.title: You prefer things just because you have seen them.
item.description: Repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus is enough to increase your positive affect toward it.

item.title: You are biologically wired to miss your own deadlines.
item.description: People consistently underestimate how long a project will take, even when they have failed to finish on time before.

item.title: The first number you hear dictates your future estimates.
item.description: A 1974 study showed that initial, irrelevant numbers significantly bias subsequent numerical estimations.

item.title: Your sense of humor relies on feeling safe.
item.description: Humor arises when a situation is perceived as a violation of social norms but is simultaneously deemed benign.

item.title: You value your own possessions more than others do.
item.description: People consistently assign a higher monetary value to an object simply because they own it.

item.title: You consistently overestimate how long you will feel hurt.
item.description: People regularly miscalculate the duration and intensity of their emotional reactions to future negative events.

item.title: You are not as good a driver as you think.
item.description: Svenson (1981) found that 93% of the U.S. student sample believed they were in the top 50% of driving skill.

item.title: A small mistake can make you more likable.
item.description: In a 1966 experiment, the 'pratfall effect' demonstrated that highly competent individuals are rated more favorably after a minor social blunder, while the same blunder causes those perceived as mediocre to be rated less favorably.

item.title: You judge decisions by the result, not the process.
item.description: A 1988 study found that observers rate a high-risk decision as more intelligent if it leads to success than if it results in failure.

item.title: Thinking about an object makes its importance grow.
item.description: In a 1998 study published in Psychological Science, Schkade and Kahneman demonstrated that people fall victim to a 'focusing illusion' when predicting their future happiness.

item.title: You prefer images of yourself when they are reversed.
item.description: A 1977 study showed that people prefer their own mirror image, while their friends prefer the standard photographic version.

item.title: You subconsciously prefer the letters in your own name.
item.description: While Pelham et al. (2002) published findings suggesting implicit egotism, those results have been widely criticized for failing to account for major confounding variables.

item.title: Common tools often become invisible when you need new uses.
item.description: A 1945 study found that participants struggled to solve problems when the necessary tools were already being used for their intended purpose.

item.title: You value a goal more when it requires significant effort.
item.description: A 1959 study demonstrated that individuals rated a discussion group as more interesting if they had to undergo an embarrassing initiation to join it.

item.title: We spend more mental energy processing bad news than good.
item.description: A 2001 review concluded that humans consistently pay more attention to, and retain, negative information over positive information.

item.title: Ease of memory leads us to overestimate rare events.
item.description: A 1973 study showed that people judge the frequency of an event by how easily they can recall examples from memory.

item.title: Others cannot see your internal emotions as clearly as you.
item.description: In a 1998 study, speakers consistently overestimated how much their audience could detect their internal anxiety or lies.

item.title: Your perception of beauty shifts based on recent comparisons.
item.description: A 1980 study found that men who viewed photographs of highly attractive models subsequently rated the attractiveness of unfamiliar female targets as less appealing.

item.title: The size of a serving unit changes how much we eat.
item.description: A 2006 study showed that people ate significantly more when snacks were presented in larger units rather than smaller, individual ones.

item.title: Moving to a warmer climate rarely improves long-term happiness.
item.description: A 1998 survey found that while Midwesterners expected Californians to be happier, there was no significant difference in reported life satisfaction between the two groups.

item.title: We consistently assume that others think like we do.
item.description: A 1977 study revealed that people are significantly more likely to assume others share their own beliefs and habits than is statistically accurate.

item.title: You can be convinced you chose the rejected option.
item.description: In a 2005 study, 75% of participants failed to notice when researchers swapped their preferred photograph for the one they had initially rejected.
